titleStmt.title: Customization for the annotation of coreference and zero anaphora in a parallel Italian-Japanese corpus

sourceDesc.p: Written for this project; derived from TEI P5 version 4.12.0.

div.head: Scope and rationale
div.p: This customization governs every file in the corpus: the Italian source text of Il trionfo della morte (1894), the eight Japanese translations, and the eight stand-off alignment files. All files use the same annotation scheme.

The customization consists of a single extension: two attributes, pos and case, are added to rs. Everything else in the corpus uses TEI P5 as published. Both attributes are given closed value lists so that annotation errors are caught by validation.

A fully conformant alternative exists: ana could point at interp elements declared in encodingDesc or in a standOff. That route was not taken because the analysis reads these two properties on every one of the 5,134 annotated referring expressions in the corpus, and a pointer indirection on each would obscure the markup without adding descriptive power. The cost of the choice is that corpus files are valid against this schema rather than against tei_all, which is why the schema is referenced from schemaRef in every file.

schemaSpec.desc: TEI P5 with two added attributes on rs for the annotation of referential form and syntactic function.

constraintSpec.desc: Every pointer in ref must resolve to a person or personGrp declared in the same document.

sch:assert.test: every $p in tokenize(normalize-space(@ref), '\s+') satisfies (starts-with($p, '#') and exists(//tei:person[@xml:id = substring($p, 2)] | //tei:personGrp[@xml:id = substring($p, 2)]))

sch:rule.sch:assert: Every value of @ref must be a '#' pointer resolving to a person or personGrp in this document. Multiple referents are expressed as space-separated pointers.

constraintSpec.desc: Zero arguments are annotated only in subject function.

sch:rule.sch:assert: pos="NULL" is annotated only for zero subjects, so @case must be 'nsubj'.

constraintSpec.desc: Reflexive and clitic pronouns occur only in object function.

sch:rule.sch:assert: pos="PRON-REFLEX" occurs only in object function, so @case must be 'obj'.

attDef.desc: records the form in which the referent is realized. The value set is deliberately coarser than a part-of-speech tagset: it distinguishes the referential strategies that the analysis compares, not the strict morphosyntactic categories of the two languages.

valItem.desc: The referent is named: a personal name or a proper-noun phrase.
The referent is realized by a common noun or noun phrase, including definite descriptions and epithets.
The referent is realized by a clitic (excluding reflexives), personal or indefinite pronoun in Italian, or by a personal pronoun in Japanese.
The referent is realized by a reflexive pronoun. Occurs in the Italian source only.

The referent is realized by a determiner. In Universal Dependencies, Italian possessives are attached as det:poss; here they are recorded as DET with case=nmod. For Japaese, this tag applies to a small set of adnominals: この, こんな, あの, あんな, その, そんな.
The referent is not overtly expressed. See the remarks on the anchoring of zero arguments below.

attDef.desc: records the syntactic function of the referring expression within its clause. The values are inspired by Universal Dependencies relation labels but the set is not UD-conformant: pred has no UD counterpart, and nmod is applied more broadly than in UD Italian. The attribute labels grammatical function, not morphological case; neither Italian nor Japanese has a morphological vocative or predicative case, and no such claim is made. The name is retained from the first version of the scheme for continuity with previously published counts.

valItem.desc: Subject of a finite predicate, whether overt or zero. In Japanese this includes the subjects of adjectival predicates and of passive constructions.
Direct or indirect object, and the complement of a preposition or postposition.
The referent modifies another nominal: genitives, possessive constructions and adnominal modifiers. Applied more broadly than UD nmod.

The referent is the predicate nominal of a copular clause. The value is a documented addition to the UD-inspired set, retained because the analysis needs to distinguish predicative from argumental mentions.

exemplum.p: An overt subject and a zero subject in the same Italian sentence, both referring to the same participant:

egXML.s: Giorgio si voltò e vide la donna.

exemplum.p: The corresponding Japanese, where the subject is zero in both clauses:

egXML.s: ジョルジォ は振り返って 見た 。

exemplum.p: A plural referent, expressed as two pointers rather than as a single composite identifier:

remarks.p: Anchoring of zero arguments. A zero subject has no textual extent, so it cannot be marked by enclosing the string that expresses it. Two encodings were available: an empty rs placed at the position where the subject would stand, or an rs enclosing the predicate whose agreement morphology identifies the referent. This project uses the second. An empty element has no anchor in the token stream, which makes it invisible to the alignment procedure; enclosing the predicate gives every annotated mention a position in the text that survives both. The predicate is thus the locus of the annotation: rs with pos=NULL asserts that an unexpressed argument of the enclosed predicate refers to the entity named in ref, and the enclosed string is a verb, not a referring expression. In Italian the predicate is always a finite verb. In Japanese it may also be an adjectival predicate or a copular phrase.

Scope. Only zero subjects are annotated. the constraint rs-null-is-subject enforces this scope decision. It records a decision about coverage, not a claim about the languages, and would need to be relaxed if object drop were brought into the annotation.
Multiple referents. Where a mention refers to more than one participant, ref carries several space-separated pointers.

constraintSpec.desc: Speaker and addressee must be given as resolvable pointers.

sch:assert.test: every $p in tokenize(normalize-space(.), '\s+') satisfies (starts-with($p, '#') and exists(//tei:person[@xml:id = substring($p, 2)] | //tei:personGrp[@xml:id = substring($p, 2)]))

sch:rule.sch:assert: @who and @toWhom take '#' pointers to person or personGrp entries. Several addressees are given as space-separated pointers.

remarks.p: Letters quoted within the narrative are encoded as q with type=written. floatingText would be the closer structural match for the longer letters, which have their own closing salutations, but it would nest a complete text inside the paragraph stream and interrupt the sequence of s elements on which the alignment depends.

constraintSpec.desc: Alignment pointers must name an s-unit in one of the aligned documents.

sch:rule.sch:assert: Every pointer in @target must end in a fragment identifier of the form prefix_N naming an s-unit.

remarks.p: Each witness uses its own s-unit identifier prefix, so the two sides of a link are distinguishable from the fragment identifier alone and s-unit identifiers are unique across the corpus. Correspondences are n:m. Only realized correspondences are recorded: sentences with no counterpart are omitted rather than linked to an empty pointer.
